**[V. RELEVANT GEOGRAPHIC MARKET]**

42\. The relevant geographic market is Sullivan County, Washington County, and Carter County, Tennessee, collectively referred to as the "Tri-County Area." The Tri-County Area has a combined population of approximately 311,000 residents and encompasses the cities of Kingsport, Johnson City, Bristol (Tennessee), and Elizabethton, among other communities.

43\. The Tri-County Area is the geographic area in which Plaintiffs and Crestline compete for the provision of orthopedic surgical services to commercial health insurers. All four of Crestline\'s acute-care hospitals are located within the Tri-County Area. AMP\'s Ridge Surgical Center is located in Johnson City, in Washington County. The vast majority of orthopedic surgical procedures performed for the commercially insured population of the Tri-County Area are performed at facilities within the Tri-County Area.

44\. Patients residing in the Tri-County Area reasonably and predominantly look to providers located within the Tri-County Area for orthopedic surgical services. The Tri-County Area is a well-defined metropolitan statistical area with its own established healthcare infrastructure, physician referral patterns, primary care networks, and patient population. The healthcare delivery system in the Tri-County Area is largely self-contained, with patients accessing the full continuum of orthopedic care --- from initial evaluation through surgery and rehabilitation --- within the geographic boundaries of the three-county region.

45\. There are approximately 372,000 commercially insured lives in the Tri-County Area, as measured by the number of individuals enrolled in commercial health insurance plans whose provider networks include Tri-County Area providers. These commercially insured individuals constitute the patient population that orthopedic surgeons in the Tri-County Area compete to serve, and their access to orthopedic surgical care is mediated by the network design decisions of the commercial health insurers described herein.

46\. The Tri-County Area is a well-defined geographic market for the provision of orthopedic surgical services sold to commercial health insurers. The concentration of healthcare facilities, physician practices, insurance networks, and patient populations within the Tri-County Area establishes it as the relevant geographic area in which competition for orthopedic surgical services to commercially insured patients takes place. The commercial health insurers that dominate the Tri-County Area market --- Blue Ridgeway, Volunteer Benefits, and Pinnacle Select --- each maintain provider networks that are designed around the Tri-County Area provider base, and their network design decisions with respect to orthopedic surgical services are made with reference to the providers and facilities located within this geographic region.

**[VI. CRESTLINE\'S MONOPOLY POWER]**

47\. Crestline performs approximately 70% of all orthopedic surgeries in the Tri-County Area, giving it an overwhelmingly dominant position in the Orthopedic Services Market. This extraordinary market share, standing alone, is sufficient to establish a prima facie case of monopoly power under Section 2 of the Sherman Act, and courts have consistently held that market shares of this magnitude give rise to an inference of monopoly power.

48\. Crestline\'s dominance in the Orthopedic Services Market is further demonstrated by its operation of four acute-care hospitals, including Crestline Regional Medical Center --- the only Level I trauma center in the Tri-County Area --- and thirty-one outpatient clinics. This vast physical infrastructure provides Crestline with unparalleled capacity to perform orthopedic surgical procedures and to serve as a comprehensive orthopedic care delivery system across the entire Tri-County Area. No other provider in the region possesses anything approaching this scale of facilities and resources.

49\. Twenty-eight of the forty-seven orthopedic surgeons practicing in the Tri-County Area --- approximately 59.6% --- are employed by or exclusively affiliated with Crestline. This concentration of orthopedic surgical talent within a single health system gives Crestline an enormous structural advantage over all competing providers and enables Crestline to offer a broader range of orthopedic sub-specialty services than any other provider in the region.

50\. AMP is the only other significant provider of orthopedic surgical services in the Tri-County Area, with twelve surgeons (the Plaintiffs herein) representing approximately 25.5% of the orthopedic surgeon workforce. AMP\'s Ridge Surgical Center is the only ambulatory surgical center in the Tri-County Area that is not owned by or affiliated with Crestline and that performs a significant volume of orthopedic surgical procedures.

51\. The remaining seven orthopedic surgeons in the Tri-County Area are independent practitioners who are not affiliated with either Crestline or AMP. These independent surgeons account for a small share of the total orthopedic surgical volume in the Tri-County Area and do not possess the scale, resources, or organizational infrastructure to effectively constrain Crestline\'s market power.

52\. Barriers to entry in the Orthopedic Services Market are high and serve to protect Crestline\'s dominant market position from competitive challenge. Entry into the market for orthopedic surgical services requires, among other things: (a) the recruitment of board-certified orthopedic surgeons, who are in limited supply nationally and who must undergo lengthy credentialing processes; (b) the construction or acquisition of specialized surgical facilities equipped with orthopedic-specific instrumentation, implant inventories, and imaging technology; (c) the establishment of hospital privileges and surgical center credentials; (d) the development of referral relationships with primary care physicians and other referring providers; (e) the negotiation of network participation agreements with commercial health insurers; and (f) the development of patient volume sufficient to sustain a viable practice. These barriers are substantial and time-consuming to overcome, effectively insulating Crestline from meaningful competitive entry in the near to medium term.

53\. Crestline\'s market position is further entrenched by its exclusive preferred-provider agreements with the three largest commercial health insurers in the Tri-County Area --- Blue Ridgeway, Volunteer Benefits, and Pinnacle Select --- which collectively cover approximately 82.5% of all commercially insured lives in the region. Through these agreements, Crestline has locked up access to the vast majority of the commercially insured patient population, making it effectively impossible for competing orthopedic surgeons to maintain viable practices that depend on commercial insurance reimbursement.

54\. The combination of Crestline\'s dominant market share, high barriers to entry, and control over insurer network access gives Crestline monopoly power in the Orthopedic Services Market --- that is, the power to control prices or exclude competition in the market for orthopedic surgical services sold to commercial health insurers in the Tri-County Area. Crestline has the ability, and has demonstrated the willingness, to exclude competing orthopedic surgeons from meaningful participation in the commercially insured market through its strategic use of the PPCAs.

55\. AMP, with its twelve affiliated orthopedic surgeons and single ambulatory surgical center (Ridge Surgical Center), lacks the scale, physical infrastructure, financial resources, and referral networks necessary to effectively constrain Crestline\'s market power. AMP operates a single facility in Johnson City, compared to Crestline\'s four hospitals and thirty-one outpatient clinics spread across three counties. The disparity in resources between Crestline and AMP is vast, and Crestline\'s anticompetitive conduct has widened this gap by diverting commercially insured patients away from AMP and toward Crestline facilities.

**[VII. THE COMMERCIAL HEALTH INSURANCE MARKET IN THE TRI-COUNTY AREA]**

56\. Three commercial health insurers dominate the Tri-County Area market and collectively control access to the vast majority of commercially insured patients in the region: Blue Ridgeway Health Plan, Inc. ("Blue Ridgeway"), Volunteer Benefits Corp. ("Volunteer Benefits"), and Pinnacle Select Insurance Co. ("Pinnacle Select"). These three insurers are the gatekeepers through which orthopedic surgeons access commercially insured patients, and their network design decisions have a direct and profound impact on the competitive dynamics in the Orthopedic Services Market.

57\. Blue Ridgeway Health Plan, Inc. is the largest commercial health insurer in the Tri-County Area, with approximately 142,000 covered lives, representing approximately 38.2% of all commercially insured lives in the region. Blue Ridgeway offers a range of commercial insurance products, including preferred provider organization ("PPO"), health maintenance organization ("HMO"), and high-deductible health plan ("HDHP") products. Blue Ridgeway is a Tennessee-domiciled health insurer with regional operations throughout East Tennessee.

58\. Volunteer Benefits Corp. is the second largest commercial health insurer in the Tri-County Area, with approximately 98,000 covered lives, representing approximately 26.3% of all commercially insured lives in the region. Volunteer Benefits offers PPO and HMO products to employers and individuals throughout the Tri-County Area and is headquartered in Knoxville, Tennessee.

59\. Pinnacle Select Insurance Co. is the third largest commercial health insurer in the Tri-County Area, with approximately 67,000 covered lives, representing approximately 18.0% of all commercially insured lives in the region. Pinnacle Select is a regional insurer that offers PPO and managed care products throughout East Tennessee and Southwest Virginia.

60\. Together, Blue Ridgeway, Volunteer Benefits, and Pinnacle Select cover approximately 307,000 individuals, representing approximately 82.5% of the approximately 372,000 total commercially insured lives in the Tri-County Area. The combined market share of these three insurers gives them outsized influence over the competitive conditions facing orthopedic surgeons in the region.

61\. The remaining approximately 17.5% of commercially insured lives in the Tri-County Area --- approximately 65,000 individuals --- are fragmented among seven smaller commercial insurers and various self-insured employer plans administered by third-party administrators. No single insurer outside the three major insurers holds more than approximately 4% of the commercially insured market. This fragmentation means that the smaller insurers, individually and collectively, cannot provide orthopedic surgeons with sufficient patient volume to sustain a viable practice in the absence of participation in the networks of the three major insurers.

62\. Inclusion in the provider networks of Blue Ridgeway, Volunteer Benefits, and Pinnacle Select is essential for orthopedic surgeons to maintain a viable practice in the Tri-County Area. Without network access to these three insurers, an orthopedic surgeon is effectively cut off from 82.5% of the commercially insured patient population. Given the economics of orthopedic surgical practice --- which require substantial fixed costs for surgical facilities, staff, equipment, and malpractice insurance --- the loss of access to such a large proportion of the commercially insured patient base is economically devastating.

63\. Commercial health insurers exercise significant control over patient access to orthopedic surgical care through a variety of managed care mechanisms, including provider network design (determining which providers are "in-network" and which are "out-of-network"), tiering (assigning in-network providers to different cost-sharing tiers), and care navigation programs (employing telephonic and digital tools to actively steer patients toward preferred providers). These mechanisms give insurers substantial power to direct patient volume toward favored providers and away from disfavored providers, regardless of the clinical quality or patient satisfaction associated with the disfavored providers\' services.

64\. Crestline, by securing exclusive preferred-provider arrangements with all three major commercial health insurers, has effectively controlled the gateway through which orthopedic surgeons access commercially insured patients in the Tri-County Area. By obtaining Tier 1 Preferred status --- with its attendant lower patient co-pays and active care navigation --- Crestline has ensured that it receives the lion\'s share of commercially insured orthopedic surgical referrals, while Plaintiffs and other non-Crestline orthopedic surgeons are relegated to a disfavored Tier 2 status that makes them economically uncompetitive.

**[VIII. CRESTLINE\'S ANTICOMPETITIVE CONDUCT --- THE PREFERRED PROVIDER COLLABORATION AGREEMENTS]**

65\. Beginning in January 2021, Crestline entered into separate Preferred Provider Collaboration Agreements ("PPCAs") with each of the three major commercial health insurers in the Tri-County Area. These agreements were the cornerstone of Crestline\'s strategy to monopolize the Orthopedic Services Market and to foreclose AMP-affiliated orthopedic surgeons, including Plaintiffs, from meaningful access to commercially insured patients.

66\. On or about January 4, 2021, Crestline executed a PPCA with Blue Ridgeway Health Plan, Inc. This was the first of the three PPCAs and established the template for the exclusive preferred-provider arrangements that would follow with the other two major insurers.

67\. On or about March 12, 2021, Crestline executed a PPCA with Volunteer Benefits Corp. The terms of this agreement were substantially similar to the Blue Ridgeway PPCA, reflecting a deliberate and coordinated strategy by Crestline to systematically lock up the commercial insurance market for orthopedic surgical services.

68\. On or about June 1, 2021, Crestline executed a PPCA with Pinnacle Select Insurance Co. With the execution of this third agreement, Crestline had secured exclusive preferred-provider status with all three major commercial health insurers in the Tri-County Area, covering approximately 82.5% of all commercially insured lives in the region.

69\. Under the PPCAs, each insurer agreed to designate Crestline facilities and Crestline-affiliated orthopedic surgeons as "Tier 1 Preferred" providers for orthopedic surgical services. This Tier 1 Preferred designation entitled Crestline-affiliated providers to the most favorable patient cost-sharing terms in each insurer\'s benefit design, making Crestline the low-cost choice for commercially insured patients seeking orthopedic surgical care.

70\. The PPCAs established a tiered co-payment structure under which patients receiving orthopedic surgical services at Crestline facilities or from Crestline-affiliated surgeons pay a co-pay of approximately \$25 per surgical encounter, while patients receiving orthopedic surgical services from non-Crestline providers --- including Plaintiffs and other AMP-affiliated surgeons, who are designated as "Tier 2" providers --- pay a co-pay of approximately \$75 per surgical encounter. This threefold differential in patient cost-sharing creates a powerful economic incentive for patients to choose Crestline-affiliated surgeons over Plaintiffs, regardless of the relative quality of care or patient preference.

71\. The PPCAs further required each of the three major commercial health insurers to implement "care navigation" programs specifically designed to "preferentially steer" their members to Crestline facilities and Crestline-affiliated surgeons for orthopedic surgical services. Under these care navigation programs, when an insured member calls the insurer\'s customer service line or uses the insurer\'s online provider directory to seek an orthopedic surgeon, the insurer\'s systems and representatives are programmed to recommend Crestline-affiliated providers first and to emphasize the cost savings associated with choosing a Tier 1 Preferred provider. These care navigation protocols actively divert patients away from Plaintiffs and toward Crestline, compounding the already-significant economic incentive created by the tiered co-pay structure.

72\. In exchange for the exclusive Tier 1 Preferred designations and the implementation of care navigation programs, Crestline agreed to provide a 22% discount off its standard commercial reimbursement rates for orthopedic surgical services to each of the three major insurers. This discount was offered as the quid pro quo for the insurers\' agreement to favor Crestline and disfavor competing orthopedic surgeons, including Plaintiffs.

73\. The PPCAs further provide that if total orthopedic surgical volume at Crestline facilities falls below 3,500 procedures per insurer-year (combined across all three insurers), Crestline may reduce the discount from 22% to 15%, thereby effectively penalizing the insurers for any shift of orthopedic surgical volume away from Crestline facilities. This volume threshold provision functions as a loyalty rebate mechanism that creates an additional economic incentive for the insurers to maintain high volumes at Crestline and to discourage patient migration to competing providers. The penalty for failing to meet the volume threshold --- a reduction of the discount by seven percentage points --- is sufficiently severe that the insurers are economically motivated to steer the maximum possible volume of orthopedic surgical patients to Crestline, further foreclosing Plaintiffs from the market.

74\. The PPCAs have initial terms of three years with automatic one-year renewal periods thereafter. Either party --- Crestline or the relevant insurer --- may terminate the agreement upon 180 days\' written notice prior to the expiration of the then-current term. The Blue Ridgeway PPCA was set to expire on January 3, 2024, but has automatically renewed for an additional one-year period. The Volunteer Benefits PPCA was set to expire on March 11, 2024, and, upon information and belief, has likewise been renewed. The Pinnacle Select PPCA was set to expire on May 31, 2024, and, upon information and belief, remains in effect.

75\. The effect of the PPCAs has been to create an exclusive dealing arrangement that has de facto locked AMP-affiliated orthopedic surgeons, including Plaintiffs, out of the commercial insurance market in the Tri-County Area. While the PPCAs do not expressly prohibit the insurers from contracting with non-Crestline providers, the combined impact of the Tier 1 Preferred designation, the tripled co-pay differential, the care navigation protocols, and the volume-threshold penalty provision has been to render Plaintiffs and other non-Crestline orthopedic surgeons effectively unable to compete for commercially insured patients.

76\. By assigning Plaintiffs and other AMP-affiliated surgeons to Tier 2 status, the PPCAs tripled the out-of-pocket costs for patients seeking to use Plaintiffs\' services. Commercially insured patients in the Tri-County Area, faced with a choice between a \$25 co-pay at a Crestline facility and a \$75 co-pay at Ridge Surgical Center, overwhelmingly choose the lower-cost option. This economic reality, combined with the active care navigation programs, has diverted the vast majority of commercially insured orthopedic surgical patients away from Plaintiffs and toward Crestline.

77\. The care navigation protocols implemented by the insurers pursuant to the PPCAs have actively and systematically directed patients away from Plaintiffs and toward Crestline facilities. Upon information and belief, the insurers\' customer service representatives are trained to recommend Crestline-affiliated orthopedic surgeons as a first option, and the insurers\' online provider directories display Crestline-affiliated surgeons in a preferential manner, with prominent "Tier 1 Preferred --- Lower Cost" designations that discourage patients from selecting Tier 2 providers such as Plaintiffs.

78\. On or about July 1, 2022, the anticompetitive effects of the PPCAs escalated further when Volunteer Benefits and Pinnacle Select went beyond the tiered co-pay structure and completely removed five of the twelve Plaintiffs from their provider networks. Specifically, Dr. Samuel T. Briggs, Dr. Caroline A. Dufresne, Dr. Angela M. Stavros, Dr. Thomas R. Pendleton, and Dr. Danielle P. Fournier were dropped from the Volunteer Benefits and Pinnacle Select networks entirely, rendering them out-of-network providers for approximately 44.3% of the commercially insured population in the Tri-County Area (26.3% Volunteer Benefits + 18.0% Pinnacle Select). 79\. As of the date of this Complaint, seven of the twelve Plaintiffs --- Dr. Vogler, Dr. Hardin, Dr. Whitmore, Dr. Yamamoto, Dr. Calhoun, Dr. Ibanez, and Dr. Oxley --- remain technically in-network with at least one of the three major commercial health insurers, but are classified as Tier 2 providers subject to the significantly higher \$75 patient co-pay. This Tier 2 designation, combined with the active care navigation programs steering patients to Crestline, renders Plaintiffs\' services economically uncompetitive with those offered by Crestline-affiliated surgeons, notwithstanding that Plaintiffs offer equal or superior quality of care.

80\. The PPCAs were entered into sequentially over a five-month period --- from January 4, 2021 through June 1, 2021 --- demonstrating a coordinated, deliberate strategy by Crestline to systematically lock up the commercial insurance market for orthopedic surgical services in the Tri-County Area. The PPCAs served no purpose other than to exclude competitors and to consolidate Crestline\'s monopoly power.

**WHITFIELD, CRANE & DOYLE LLP**

**INTERNAL MEMORANDUM**

**ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL** **ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**TO:** Victoria P. Stanhope, Partner

**FROM: David A. Kestner, Senior Associate**

**DATE:** June 14, 2024

**RE:** *Vogler, et al. v. Crestline Health Systems, Inc.*, Case No. 2:24-cv-00419-CTM (E.D. Tenn., Greeneville Div.) --- Legal Standards Applicable to Defendant\'s Rule 12(b)(6) Motion to Dismiss

*This memorandum is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. Do not distribute outside the firm without authorization.*

**[I. Introduction and Purpose]**

This memorandum has been prepared in connection with the defense of our client, Crestline Health Systems, Inc. ("Crestline" or "Defendant"), against the Complaint filed on March 15, 2024, by Dr. Nathan J. Vogler, M.D., and eleven other orthopedic surgeons (collectively, "Plaintiffs"). Plaintiffs are independent orthopedic surgeons formerly or currently affiliated with Appalachian Medical Partners ("AMP"), a competing multi-specialty physician group. Plaintiffs are represented by Harrison P. Farnsworth of Farnsworth & Gault, PLLC, Johnson City, Tennessee. Crestline retained Whitfield, Crane & Doyle LLP on May 20, 2024. The deadline to file a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) is July 8, 2024.

The Complaint asserts three federal antitrust claims: (1) monopolization under Section 2 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2 (Count I); (2) attempted monopolization under Section 2 of the Sherman Act (Count II); and (3) unreasonable restraint of trade under Section 1 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1 (Count III). All three claims arise from Crestline\'s execution of Preferred Provider Collaboration Agreements ("PPCAs") with three commercial health insurers operating in the Tri-County Area of northeastern Tennessee: Blue Ridgeway Health Plan, Inc., Volunteer Benefits Corp., and Pinnacle Select Insurance Co. The PPCAs establish a tiered copay structure under which Crestline-affiliated orthopedic providers are designated as Tier 1 (preferred) providers, with a \$25 patient copay, while non-Crestline providers are assigned to Tier 2, with a \$75 patient copay. Plaintiffs allege that this tiered arrangement constitutes exclusionary conduct that forecloses them from the commercially insured orthopedic services market in the Tri-County Area. Plaintiffs seek treble damages of \$30.9 million (\$10.3 million in actual damages multiplied by three under 15 U.S.C. § 15), together with injunctive relief.

The purpose of this memorandum is to summarize the legal standards governing a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, the substantive elements of each antitrust claim asserted in the Complaint, and the doctrines relevant to the specific arguments we anticipate raising in Crestline\'s motion. Specifically, this memorandum addresses: (A) the *Twombly*/*Iqbal* pleading standard; (B) the elements of monopolization and attempted monopolization under Sherman Act § 2; (C) the elements of unreasonable restraint of trade under Sherman Act § 1; (D) the exclusive dealing doctrine; (E) market definition requirements at the pleading stage; (F) antitrust injury and standing; and (G) the application of these standards to the specific allegations in the Complaint. Each section identifies the doctrinal framework, relevant Sixth Circuit authority, and the specific vulnerabilities in the Complaint that our motion should target.

**[II. The Rule 12(b)(6) Standard Under \*Twombly\* and \*Iqbal\*]**

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) permits dismissal of a complaint where it "fail\[s\] to state a claim upon which relief can be granted." The modern standard for evaluating the sufficiency of a complaint was established by the Supreme Court in *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and refined in *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009). Together, these decisions replaced the permissive "no set of facts" standard that had governed federal pleading since *Conley v. Gibson*, 355 U.S. 41, 45-46 (1957).

In *Twombly*, the Court held that a complaint must contain "enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." 550 U.S. at 570. A claim has facial plausibility "when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged." *Id.* at 556. Mere "labels and conclusions," "a formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action," or "naked assertion\[s\] devoid of further factual enhancement" are insufficient. *Id.* at 555, 557. Significantly, *Twombly* arose in the antitrust context: the Court held that allegations of parallel conduct among telecommunications companies, without additional factual allegations from which a conspiracy could plausibly be inferred, failed to state a claim under Sherman Act § 1. *Id.* at 554-57. The decision recognized the extraordinary costs of antitrust discovery and the importance of the pleading stage as a gatekeeper to prevent meritless antitrust claims from proceeding to expensive fact-finding.

In *Iqbal*, the Court extended the *Twombly* plausibility standard to all civil actions and articulated a two-pronged analytical approach. 556 U.S. at 678-79. First, the court must identify and disregard allegations that are merely conclusory --- that is, legal conclusions couched as factual assertions. *Id.* at 678. Second, the court must evaluate the remaining well-pleaded factual allegations to determine whether they plausibly give rise to an entitlement to relief. *Id.* at 679. Plausibility demands more than a "sheer possibility" of unlawful conduct; "where a complaint pleads facts that are merely consistent with a defendant\'s liability, it stops short of the line between possibility and plausibility of entitlement to relief." *Id.* at 678 (internal quotation marks omitted).

The Sixth Circuit has faithfully applied *Twombly* and *Iqbal* to antitrust complaints and has recognized that antitrust claims receive particularly close scrutiny at the pleading stage. In *Total Benefits Planning Agency, Inc. v. Anthem Blue Cross & Blue Shield*, 552 F.3d 430, 434-36 (6th Cir. 2008), the court affirmed dismissal of antitrust claims under *Twombly* where the complaint alleged exclusionary conduct but failed to plead factual content supporting the inference of anticompetitive effects in a properly defined relevant market. Similarly, in *In re Southeastern Milk Antitrust Litigation*, 739 F.3d 262, 271-75 (6th Cir. 2014), the court applied the *Twombly*/*Iqbal* framework to antitrust intent allegations, holding that conclusory recitations of conspiratorial intent must be disregarded and that the remaining factual allegations must independently support the inference of an unlawful agreement.

It is well established that while the court accepts well-pleaded factual allegations as true on a 12(b)(6) motion, it need not accept legal conclusions, nor must it credit allegations that are contradicted by other allegations in the same complaint or by matters of which the court may take judicial notice. *See Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678; *Hendy v. Losse*, 819 F.2d 1441, 1444 (9th Cir. 1987). Similarly, the court need not accept as true allegations that are contradicted by documents incorporated by reference into the complaint. *See Weiner v. Klais & Co.*, 108 F.3d 86, 89 (6th Cir. 1997).

This principle bears directly on our motion. The Complaint contains internally inconsistent market share allegations: Paragraph 47 alleges that Crestline controls "approximately 70%" of orthopedic procedures in the alleged relevant market, while Paragraph 83 alleges that Crestline captures "over 60%" of orthopedic revenue. These figures are neither consistent with each other nor trivially reconcilable --- they purport to measure different quantities (procedures versus revenue) without explaining the basis for the divergence. Under *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, a complaint that offers contradictory allegations regarding a critical element of the claim undermines its own plausibility. The court is not required to credit one allegation over the other when the complaint itself fails to provide a coherent factual basis for either. This internal contradiction goes to the heart of the monopoly power analysis and should be highlighted in our motion.

**[III. Elements of Sherman Act § 2 Claims]**

**[A. Monopolization (Count I)]**

Section 2 of the Sherman Act provides that "\[e\]very person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize . . . any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony." 15 U.S.C. § 2. A private plaintiff may enforce this provision through a treble damages action under Section 4 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15.

A monopolization claim requires proof of two elements: "(1) the possession of monopoly power in the relevant market and (2) the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power as distinguished from growth or development as a consequence of a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident." *United States v. Grinnell Corp.*, 384 U.S. 563, 570-71 (1966). Both elements must be adequately alleged at the pleading stage.

**Monopoly Power.** Monopoly power is "the power to control prices or exclude competition." *Eastman Kodak Co. v. Image Technical Services, Inc.*, 504 U.S. 451, 481 (1992) (quoting *United States v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co.*, 351 U.S. 377, 391 (1956)). It may be proven directly --- through evidence that the defendant has actually controlled prices or excluded competitors --- or it may be inferred circumstantially from a predominant share of a properly defined relevant market coupled with the existence of significant barriers to entry. *Id.*; *Grinnell*, 384 U.S. at 571.

The circumstantial inference of monopoly power from market share is not automatic. Courts have consistently held that a market share below 50% is insufficient as a matter of law to support an inference of monopoly power. *See Dimmitt Agri Industries, Inc. v. CPC International, Inc.*, 679 F.2d 516, 529 (5th Cir. 1982); *Exxon Corp. v. Berwick Bay Real Estate Partners*, 748 F.2d 937, 940 (5th Cir. 1984). Market shares between 50% and 70% are generally held insufficient standing alone to support the inference, absent substantial additional evidence of barriers to entry or other indicia of market power. The weight of authority suggests that market shares below 75% are per se insufficient to establish monopoly power absent compelling additional evidence of barriers to entry and the defendant\'s ability to exclude competition. *See Bailey v. Allgas, Inc.*, 284 F.3d 1237, 1250 (11th Cir. 2002) (noting that a share "above 70%" is "generally required" to infer monopoly power); *Dimmitt Agri Industries*, 679 F.2d at 529 (similar); *American Tobacco Co. v. United States*, 328 U.S. 781 (1946) (finding monopoly power at approximately 68%, but in context of extensive additional evidence of exclusionary conduct and coordinated behavior). The critical takeaway from these authorities is that monopoly power is not plausibly alleged simply by claiming a market share in the 60-70% range without detailed factual allegations of barriers to entry, pricing control, or the ability to exclude competitors from the relevant market.

**Exclusionary Conduct.** The second element of a monopolization claim --- willful acquisition or maintenance of monopoly power --- requires proof that the defendant engaged in exclusionary or anticompetitive conduct. Not all hard competition is exclusionary. Conduct that reflects "competition on the merits" --- including aggressive pricing, vigorous discounting, offering superior contract terms, and improving service quality --- does not violate Section 2 even if it causes harm to competitors. *Verizon Communications Inc. v. Law Offices of Curtis V. Trinko, LLP*, 540 U.S. 398, 407-08 (2004). The conduct must be shown to "tend\[\] to impair the opportunities of rivals" in a manner that does not merely reflect "growth or development as a consequence of a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident." *Grinnell*, 384 U.S. at 571. The Sixth Circuit has addressed this distinction in *Conwood Co. v. United States Tobacco Co.*, 290 F.3d 768, 783-84 (6th Cir. 2002), applying the framework from *Grinnell* and requiring evidence that the defendant\'s conduct went beyond the bounds of normal competitive behavior.

**Application to This Case.** The Complaint\'s inconsistent market share allegations --- approximately 70% of procedures (¶ 47) versus over 60% of revenue (¶ 83) --- raise a threshold question of whether either figure, even taken in the light most favorable to Plaintiffs, is sufficient to establish monopoly power. The higher figure (approximately 70%) falls at the margins of what courts have found sufficient, and the lower figure (over 60%) is almost certainly insufficient standing alone. The Complaint offers no meaningful allegations regarding barriers to entry --- indeed, it acknowledges that four independent orthopedic surgeons have obtained Tier 1 status by entering into individual agreements with the insurers (Complaint ¶ 39), which suggests that barriers to entry into the Tier 1 network are low. These inconsistencies and omissions undermine the plausibility of the monopoly power allegation, and we should argue that Count I fails at the first element.

**[B. Attempted Monopolization (Count II)]**

An attempted monopolization claim under Sherman Act § 2 requires proof of three elements: "(1) that the defendant has engaged in predatory or anticompetitive conduct with (2) a specific intent to monopolize and (3) a dangerous probability of achieving monopoly power." *Spectrum Sports, Inc. v. McQuillan*, 506 U.S. 447, 456 (1993).

**Specific Intent.** The specific intent element requires more than an intent to compete vigorously or to gain a competitive advantage. The plaintiff must demonstrate a deliberate intention to destroy competition or to achieve monopoly power through anticompetitive means. *Spectrum Sports*, 506 U.S. at 459. Specific intent may sometimes be inferred from conduct, but only where the conduct "is of a kind clearly threatening to competition or clearly exclusionary" and has no legitimate business rationale. *Id.* Where the challenged conduct carries procompetitive justifications --- such as offering volume discounts in exchange for preferred provider status, or structuring tiered pricing arrangements that reduce costs for consumers --- an inference of anticompetitive intent is not plausible without additional direct evidence of the defendant\'s subjective desire to achieve monopoly power through exclusionary means.

Under *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, bare conclusory allegations of intent are legal conclusions entitled to no weight. A complaint that merely recites that the "defendant acted with the specific intent to monopolize the relevant market" has stated a legal conclusion, not a factual allegation. The Sixth Circuit applied this principle in *In re Southeastern Milk Antitrust Litigation*, 739 F.3d 262, 271-75 (6th Cir. 2014), holding that conclusory recitations of anticompetitive intent must be disregarded at the pleading stage and that the remaining factual allegations must independently give rise to a plausible inference of the requisite mental state. The factual allegations must describe conduct or communications from which a trier of fact could reasonably conclude that the defendant harbored the specific intent to achieve monopoly power through anticompetitive means, as opposed to the ordinary intent to compete and prevail in the marketplace.

**Dangerous Probability.** The dangerous probability element requires demonstration that the defendant had a "realistic probability" of achieving monopoly power in a properly defined relevant market. *Spectrum Sports*, 506 U.S. at 456. This element incorporates the same market definition and market power considerations discussed above in connection with the monopolization claim, though the threshold may be somewhat lower since the claim does not require proof of actual monopoly power. Nonetheless, a properly defined relevant market remains essential --- without it, there is no framework within which to assess the probability of achieving monopoly power. *Id.* at 459 ("without a definition of \[the relevant\] market there is no way to measure \[the defendant\'s\] ability to lessen or destroy competition").

**Application to This Case.** The Complaint\'s attempted monopolization claim is particularly vulnerable on the specific intent element. The Complaint effectively concedes the absence of direct evidence of anticompetitive intent --- there are no allegations of internal memoranda, emails, board resolutions, strategic plans, or executive communications evidencing a purpose to exclude competitors from the market. The allegations of intent are entirely inferential, drawn from the timing and structure of the PPCAs themselves. But entering into discount agreements with willing insurer counterparties --- agreements that produce lower copays for consumers --- is quintessential procompetitive conduct. It is the type of vigorous competition the antitrust laws are designed to encourage, not to prohibit. Under *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, inferring anticompetitive intent from conduct that is manifestly procompetitive requires "something more" --- additional factual allegations that render the inference of anticompetitive purpose plausible despite the obvious procompetitive explanation. The Complaint lacks any such additional factual content. This gap is fatal to Count II.

The dangerous probability element is equally deficient, because it depends on the same flawed market definition and inconsistent market share allegations that afflict Count I. If the Complaint fails to plausibly allege monopoly power, it a fortiori fails to allege a dangerous probability of achieving monopoly power.

**[IV. Elements of Sherman Act § 1 Claims]**

**[A. General Framework]**

Section 1 of the Sherman Act provides that "\[e\]very contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal." 15 U.S.C. § 1. A private plaintiff alleging a Section 1 violation must establish three elements: (1) the existence of an agreement --- a contract, combination, or conspiracy --- between two or more legally distinct entities; (2) that the agreement unreasonably restrains trade; and (3) that the restraint affects interstate commerce. *See Monsanto Co. v. Spray-Rite Service Corp.*, 465 U.S. 752, 761 (1984); *Standard Oil Co. v. United States*, 221 U.S. 1, 59-60 (1911).

The agreement requirement is the foundational element of a Section 1 claim. Section 1 does not reach unilateral conduct --- "independent action is not proscribed." *Monsanto*, 465 U.S. at 761. The agreement may be express or implied, but its existence must be supported by factual allegations sufficient to make the inference of concerted action plausible under *Twombly*. 550 U.S. at 553-57. In this case, the Complaint alleges that the PPCAs themselves constitute the agreements in restraint of trade --- that is, the contracts between Crestline and the three insurers. The existence of the agreements is not in dispute. The question is whether they unreasonably restrain trade, which in turn depends on the nature of the agreements, the analytical framework applied, and the specific anticompetitive effects alleged.

**[B. Vertical vs. Horizontal Agreements and the Rule of Reason]**

The analytical framework applicable to a Section 1 claim depends critically on whether the challenged agreement is horizontal (between competitors) or vertical (between entities at different levels of the supply chain). After *Leegin Creative Leather Products, Inc. v. PSKS, Inc.*, 551 U.S. 877 (2007), virtually all vertical restraints are evaluated under the rule of reason rather than treated as per se illegal. The per se rule --- which condemns certain categories of agreements as inherently anticompetitive without requiring proof of actual market effects --- is reserved for a narrow class of horizontal restraints, principally price-fixing, market allocation, and bid-rigging among competitors. *See Texaco Inc. v. Dagher*, 547 U.S. 1, 5 (2006); *Leegin*, 551 U.S. at 886-87.

The PPCAs at issue in this case are vertical agreements between Crestline, a provider of orthopedic services, and three health insurers, which are purchasers of those provider services on behalf of their enrollees. There is no allegation anywhere in the Complaint that Crestline entered into a horizontal agreement with any competing provider --- neither with AMP nor with any individual independent surgeon --- to divide markets, allocate patients, fix prices, or otherwise restrict competition. The agreements run exclusively along the vertical axis of the healthcare delivery chain: provider to payer. As vertical restraints, the PPCAs must be evaluated under the rule of reason.

The rule of reason analysis requires a comprehensive assessment of the restraint\'s net competitive effects. *See National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Alston*, 594 U.S. 69, 84-85 (2021); *Ohio v. American Express Co.*, 585 U.S. 529, 541-42 (2018). The inquiry considers: (a) the nature of the restraint and its likely effect on competition in the relevant market; (b) the definition of the relevant market, including both product and geographic dimensions; (c) the defendant\'s market power within that market; (d) procompetitive justifications for the restraint; and (e) the availability of less restrictive alternatives that would achieve the same procompetitive benefits. The plaintiff bears the initial burden of demonstrating that the restraint produces significant anticompetitive effects in the relevant market --- that is, effects on competition as a whole, not merely harm to the plaintiff as an individual competitor. *See American Express*, 585 U.S. at 541-42.

At the pleading stage, the complaint must allege facts sufficient to plausibly state that the restraint produces net anticompetitive effects in a properly defined relevant market. This is a demanding standard in the context of vertical arrangements, because vertical restraints often produce significant procompetitive benefits --- including lower prices, improved service, and expanded output --- that must be weighed against any alleged anticompetitive effects. A complaint that alleges only harm to the plaintiff, without factual allegations of harm to consumers or to the competitive process, fails to satisfy this standard.

The Complaint does not allege a horizontal agreement of any kind. The PPCAs are vertical agreements. Accordingly, Plaintiffs\' Section 1 claim must satisfy the rule of reason\'s heightened analytical burden, which demands factual allegations of actual or likely anticompetitive effects in the relevant market --- not merely allegations of competitive injury to the Plaintiffs themselves. As we discuss in Section VI below, the Complaint\'s failure to allege any consumer harm --- no price increases, no quality reductions, no output decreases --- is a critical deficiency in this regard.

**[C. The Exclusive Dealing Doctrine]**

Exclusive dealing arrangements are a species of vertical restraint evaluated under the rule of reason. *Tampa Electric Co. v. Nashville Coal Co.*, 365 U.S. 320, 327-28 (1961). The Complaint characterizes the PPCAs as de facto exclusive dealing arrangements. Whether this characterization is legally supportable is a central question for our motion.

Under *Tampa Electric*, the legality of an exclusive dealing arrangement is assessed by considering the totality of the circumstances, with particular emphasis on the following factors: (1) the degree of foreclosure in the relevant market --- that is, the share of the market from which competitors are excluded by the arrangement (courts have generally required foreclosure of a "substantial share" of the market, typically 30-40% or more); (2) the duration and terminability of the agreement; (3) the existence of procompetitive justifications for the arrangement; and (4) whether the arrangement actually excludes competitors from the market or merely provides the defendant with a competitive advantage. *Tampa Electric*, 365 U.S. at 327-29; *see also Jefferson Parish Hospital District No. 2 v. Hyde*, 466 U.S. 2, 45 (1984) (O\'Connor, J., concurring) (articulating factors for evaluating exclusive dealing).

**Duration and Terminability Are Critical Factors.** The duration of an exclusive dealing arrangement and the ease with which it may be terminated are among the most important considerations in assessing its competitive effects. In *Tampa Electric*, the Supreme Court found a twenty-year exclusive supply agreement lawful because, notwithstanding its lengthy term, it foreclosed only a small share of the relevant market. 365 U.S. at 334-35. Lower courts have consistently emphasized that short-term, easily terminable exclusive dealing agreements present far less anticompetitive concern than long-term arrangements that lock in counterparties. In *CDC Technologies, Inc. v. IDEXX Laboratories, Inc.*, 186 F.3d 74, 80 (2d Cir. 1999), the Second Circuit held that exclusive dealing agreements terminable on short notice are "presumptively lawful" because customers remain free to switch suppliers when the arrangement no longer serves their interests. The Ninth Circuit reached a similar conclusion in *Omega Environmental, Inc. v. Gilbarco, Inc.*, 127 F.3d 1157, 1164 (9th Cir. 1997), holding that terminable-at-will exclusive dealing agreements present "much less cause for anticompetitive concern." And in *Concord Boat Corp. v. Brunswick Corp.*, 207 F.3d 1039, 1059 (8th Cir. 2000), the Eighth Circuit held that one-year dealer agreements with volume-based discounts did not constitute anticompetitive exclusive dealing, in part because customers could switch to competitors at the end of any annual period.

**Distinction Between Exclusive Dealing and Preferential Tiering.** A critical threshold question in this case is whether the PPCAs constitute "exclusive dealing" at all. True exclusive dealing requires that the contract actually foreclose rivals from the relevant market --- that is, prohibit the counterparty from dealing with competitors of the defendant. If the agreement merely grants the defendant preferential status --- for example, a lower copay tier, preferred listing in provider directories, or directed patient steering --- while leaving the counterparty free to contract with competitors, it does not constitute "exclusive" dealing in the antitrust sense. The Sixth Circuit has recognized that preferential arrangements, which do not bar the counterparty from dealing with rivals, do not automatically constitute exclusive dealing and must be analyzed on their own terms under the rule of reason. The distinction is vital: preferential tiering incentivizes consumers to choose the preferred provider through price differentials but does not compel them to do so and does not prohibit the payer from maintaining contractual relationships with non-preferred providers.

This distinction is directly relevant to the PPCAs. The Complaint itself acknowledges (¶ 34) that the PPCAs establish a tiered copay structure: \$25 for Tier 1 (Crestline-affiliated) providers and \$75 for Tier 2 (non-Crestline) providers. The PPCAs do not, by their terms, prohibit Blue Ridgeway, Volunteer Benefits, or Pinnacle Select from including non-Crestline orthopedic providers in their networks. Indeed, the Complaint concedes that seven of the twelve Plaintiff surgeons remain "technically" in-network with at least one of the three major insurers (

Complaint ¶ 41). Moreover, four independent orthopedic surgeons --- not affiliated with Crestline or AMP --- have obtained Tier 1 preferred status by negotiating individual agreements with the insurers (Complaint ¶ 39). This is preferential tiering, not exclusive dealing. The PPCAs create competitive advantages for Crestline, but they do not foreclose rivals from the market.

The PPCAs have initial three-year terms with automatic one-year renewals, terminable by either party on 180 days\' notice (Complaint ¶ 36). Under the case law discussed above, this is a relatively short-term, easily terminable arrangement. The six-month termination window means that any insurer dissatisfied with the arrangement --- or any insurer that receives a superior offer from a competing provider group --- can exit the PPCA within a commercially reasonable time frame. This feature substantially undermines any argument that the PPCAs produce the type of durable market foreclosure that the exclusive dealing doctrine is designed to address.

**[V. Relevant Market Definition at the Pleading Stage]**

A properly defined relevant market is an essential predicate for both Section 1 and Section 2 claims where the claim depends on market power, monopoly power, or foreclosure. Without a coherent market definition, "there is no way to measure \[the defendant\'s\] ability to lessen or destroy competition." *Spectrum Sports*, 506 U.S. at 459; *see also Walker Process Equipment, Inc. v. Food Machinery & Chemical Corp.*, 382 U.S. 172, 177 (1965). The relevant market has two dimensions: the product market and the geographic market.

**Product Market.** The product market is defined by reference to the "reasonable interchangeability" of products or services from the consumer\'s perspective. *United States v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co.* ("*Cellophane*"), 351 U.S. 377, 395 (1956). The modern economic approach employs the "hypothetical monopolist test," also known as the SSNIP (Small but Significant Non-transitory Increase in Price) test: would a hypothetical monopolist controlling all products in the proposed market find it profitable to impose a small but significant non-transitory increase in price (typically 5-10%)? If a sufficient number of consumers would respond by switching to products or services outside the proposed market, rendering the price increase unprofitable, the proposed market is too narrowly defined and must be expanded to include the substitutes. *See* U.S. Department of Justice & Federal Trade Commission, Horizontal Merger Guidelines § 4.1 (2023).

Market definition is ordinarily a question of fact, but a complaint may be dismissed at the pleading stage where it alleges a facially implausible market definition that fails to account for obvious substitutes. The Sixth Circuit has held that market definition can be tested on a motion to dismiss. *Re/Max International, Inc. v. Realty One, Inc.*, 173 F.3d 995, 1016 (6th Cir. 1999) (affirming dismissal in part on deficient market definition); *see also Todd v. Exxon Corp.*, 275 F.3d 191, 199-200 (2d Cir. 2001) (Sotomayor, J.) (permitting challenge to market definition at pleading stage while recognizing that the issue is "typically a factual inquiry").

The Complaint defines the relevant product market as "commercially insured orthopedic surgery and related services in the Tri-County Area" (Complaint ¶ 44). This definition explicitly excludes orthopedic procedures paid for by government payers --- Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and Veterans Health Administration --- as well as self-pay patients. According to data referenced in the Complaint itself (¶ 46), government payers account for approximately 44% of all orthopedic procedures performed in the Tri-County Area. The Complaint offers no justification for excluding this substantial volume of interchangeable services from the product market. The same surgeons performing the same total knee arthroplasties, rotator cuff repairs, and spinal fusions on commercially insured patients also perform identical procedures on Medicare and Medicaid patients. The surgical technique, the operating room, the hospital facility, the equipment, and the surgeon\'s time and expertise are the same regardless of the payer source. A hypothetical monopolist of commercially insured orthopedic services could not profitably impose a significant price increase if surgeons could shift capacity to serve government-payer and self-pay patients (and consumers could seek care from providers focused on those payer populations). The exclusion of 44% of orthopedic procedures from the product market is an artificial narrowing that inflates Crestline\'s apparent market share and renders the product market definition facially deficient.

Courts have rejected product market definitions that artificially exclude interchangeable services in order to inflate market share or market concentration. The failure to include all reasonable substitutes within the market definition is a recognized basis for dismissal at the pleading stage. We should argue that the Complaint\'s exclusion of government-payer orthopedic services is analytically unjustified and that, when these services are properly included, Crestline\'s share of the broader orthopedic services market drops substantially, undermining the monopoly power and foreclosure allegations.

**Geographic Market.** The geographic market must "correspond to the commercial realities of the industry and be economically significant." *Brown Shoe Co. v. United States*, 370 U.S. 294, 336-37 (1962). It encompasses "the area of effective competition . . . \[the\] area in which the seller operates, and to which the purchaser can practicably turn for supplies." *Tampa Electric*, 365 U.S. at 327. A plaintiff cannot gerrymander a geographic market by drawing boundaries that exclude readily accessible competitive alternatives. The relevant inquiry is whether consumers (here, patients) could practically obtain orthopedic services from providers located outside the proposed geographic boundary.

The Complaint defines the geographic market as the Tri-County Area --- Sullivan, Washington, and Carter Counties, Tennessee (Complaint ¶ 45). However, the Complaint makes no allegation explaining why patients in the Tri-County Area could not reasonably seek orthopedic care from providers in adjacent geographic areas. Bristol, Virginia, and Abingdon, Virginia, are located approximately 25 miles north of Johnson City and are home to at least three orthopedic practices, including Ballad Health-affiliated providers operating at Johnston Memorial Hospital. Asheville, North Carolina, approximately 65 miles southeast, is a regional medical hub with multiple orthopedic surgery groups and two major hospital systems. The Complaint is silent on the question of cross-border competition. It offers no allegations regarding patient travel patterns, insurer network boundaries that prevent access to out-of-area providers, or any other facts that would justify limiting the geographic market to the three Tennessee counties. This silence is a significant vulnerability. We should argue that the geographic market is gerrymandered to exclude accessible alternatives and that, when properly expanded to include the Bristol/Abingdon corridor and the Asheville market, Crestline\'s share of the relevant geographic market diminishes materially.

**[VI. Antitrust Injury and Standing]**

**[A. Antitrust Injury]**

Under Section 4 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15, a private antitrust plaintiff must demonstrate "antitrust injury" --- "injury of the type the antitrust laws were intended to prevent and that flows from that which makes defendants\' acts unlawful." *Brunswick Corp. v. Pueblo Bowl-O-Mat, Inc.*, 429 U.S. 477, 489 (1977). The antitrust injury requirement serves as a critical filter that ensures the antitrust laws are used to protect the competitive process --- not to provide a remedy for every form of economic loss that a competitor may suffer in the marketplace.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that the antitrust laws "were enacted for the protection of competition, not competitors." *Brown Shoe Co. v. United States*, 370 U.S. 294, 320 (1962); *Brunswick*, 429 U.S. at 488. This principle has direct application to cases in which a plaintiff alleges lost revenue or market share but fails to allege harm to consumers or to the competitive process itself. Lost revenue to a competitor is not automatically an antitrust injury. The injury must reflect harm to the competitive process --- manifested through higher prices to consumers, reduced output, diminished quality or innovation, or restriction of consumer choice. *See Atlantic Richfield Co. v. USA Petroleum Co.*, 495 U.S. 328, 334 (1990).

The Sixth Circuit has rigorously applied the antitrust injury requirement. In *NicSand, Inc. v. 3M Co.*, 507 F.3d 442, 450-52 (6th Cir. 2007) (en banc), the court dismissed a Section 2 claim where the plaintiff alleged lost market share resulting from the defendant\'s exclusive dealing arrangements with retailers, but failed to allege any harm to consumers --- no price increases, no quality reductions, no output limitations. The court emphasized that the plaintiff\'s injury --- loss of shelf space and sales --- was harm to a competitor, not harm to competition. The en banc decision made clear that the antitrust injury requirement is a substantive element of a private antitrust claim that must be adequately alleged at the pleading stage and can serve as a basis for dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6).

The Complaint in this case alleges that the twelve Plaintiff surgeons suffered a combined revenue decline of \$10.3 million over a three-year period --- from \$18.2 million in 2020 to \$7.9 million in 2023 (Complaint ¶¶ 56-58). This is the entirety of the alleged injury. The Complaint does not allege any harm to consumers in the Tri-County Area. There is no allegation that orthopedic surgery prices have increased --- indeed, the PPCAs appear to have reduced patient copays from a previous uniform level to \$25 for Tier 1 providers. There is no allegation that the quality of orthopedic care has diminished. There is no allegation that the total volume of orthopedic procedures in the Tri-County Area has declined or that patient access to orthopedic services has been restricted in any meaningful way. The injury alleged is exclusively competitive harm to the Plaintiffs as individual business enterprises --- precisely the type of "competitor harm" that *Brunswick* and its progeny hold insufficient to establish antitrust injury. This deficiency pervades all three Counts and provides an independent basis for dismissal of the entire Complaint.

**[B. Antitrust Standing --- The AGC Efficient Enforcer Factors]**

Even where antitrust injury can be established, a private plaintiff must also demonstrate antitrust standing --- that is, that the plaintiff is a proper party to enforce the antitrust laws and recover damages. The Supreme Court addressed the standing requirement in *Associated General Contractors of California, Inc. v. California State Council of Carpenters*, 459 U.S. 519, 535-45 (1983) ("*AGC*"), establishing a multi-factor test to determine whether a plaintiff is an "efficient enforcer" of the antitrust laws.

The *AGC* factors include: (1) the causal connection between the alleged antitrust violation and the plaintiff\'s harm; (2) the nature of the alleged injury, including whether it is the type the antitrust laws were intended to redress; (3) the directness or indirectness of the asserted injury; (4) the existence of more direct victims of the anticompetitive conduct who could sue; (5) the potential for duplicative recovery if the plaintiff and other injured parties all bring suit; and (6) the risk of complex apportionment of damages among multiple plaintiffs. *Id.* at 537-45. These factors are not a rigid checklist but a flexible inquiry designed to identify the most efficient enforcer --- the party whose injury is most directly linked to the violation and whose suit is most likely to vindicate the purposes of the antitrust laws.

The Sixth Circuit has consistently applied the *AGC* factors in evaluating antitrust standing. In *Southaven Land Co. v. Malone & Hyde, Inc.*, 715 F.2d 1079, 1084-85 (6th Cir. 1983), the court analyzed each factor to determine whether a landlord had standing to challenge anticompetitive conduct that directly injured its tenant. In *In re Cardizem CD Antitrust Litigation*, 332 F.3d 896, 909-12 (6th Cir. 2003), the court evaluated whether indirect purchasers --- consumers who purchased pharmaceutical products through intermediaries --- were efficient enforcers of the antitrust laws.

Application of the *AGC* factors to the Plaintiffs in this case raises serious questions about their antitrust standing.

The twelve Plaintiff surgeons are individual orthopedic physicians who practiced as independent contractors affiliated with AMP. They were not parties to the PPCAs --- the PPCAs were executed between Crestline and the three insurers. The insurers\' subsequent decisions to implement tiered copay structures, to classify certain providers as Tier 2, or to alter network participation criteria were independent business judgments made by the insurers, not by Crestline. The causal chain between Crestline\'s execution of the PPCAs and the Plaintiffs\' alleged revenue losses runs through multiple intermediate steps: Crestline negotiated PPCAs with insurers; insurers implemented tiered structures; patients responded to copay differentials by shifting to Tier 1 providers; Plaintiffs\' patient volumes declined as a result. Each step involves independent decision-making by third parties (insurers and patients).

Under *AGC* Factor 3 (directness), the Plaintiffs\' injury is indirect. It flows not from Crestline\'s conduct directed at Plaintiffs, but from the insurers\' network design decisions --- decisions over which the insurers exercised independent judgment. Crestline did not terminate Plaintiffs from any network, did not set their copay levels, and did not control patient referral patterns. The directness of the injury is attenuated by the intervening conduct of the insurer counterparties.

Under *AGC* Factor 4 (more direct victims), AMP is a far more direct victim of the alleged anticompetitive conduct. AMP is the institutional provider with direct contractual relationships with the three insurers. AMP\'s contracts with the insurers were directly affected by the PPCAs. AMP suffered institutional competitive harm as a provider group. Yet AMP chose not to join this lawsuit. When a more direct victim exists and has elected not to sue, courts are less inclined to find that more remote parties --- here, individual surgeons affiliated with AMP --- are efficient enforcers. The Plaintiffs\' decision to sue as individuals, rather than through AMP, may have been strategic, but it creates a standing problem under *AGC*.

Under *AGC* Factor 5 (duplicative recovery), permitting the individual surgeons to recover treble damages of \$30.9 million does not preclude AMP from subsequently filing its own antitrust action seeking damages for the same competitive harm. The potential for duplicative recovery is significant and weighs against standing.

Under *AGC* Factor 6 (complex apportionment), the Complaint seeks aggregate damages on behalf of twelve individual surgeons who practiced at varying levels of volume, in varying orthopedic subspecialties (hip and knee arthroplasty, sports medicine, spinal surgery, hand and wrist), with varying payer mixes, and with varying degrees of continued in-network status. Apportioning the \$10.3 million aggregate revenue decline among twelve individual plaintiffs --- each of whom experienced different competitive dynamics --- presents substantial complexity that counsels against treating these individuals as efficient enforcers.

Taken together, these factors suggest that the individual surgeon-Plaintiffs may lack antitrust standing as efficient enforcers of the antitrust laws, even if antitrust injury could otherwise be shown. This argument applies across all three Counts and should be included in our motion as an alternative basis for dismissal.

**[VII. Application to the Vogler Complaint --- Summary of Recommended Arguments]**

This section synthesizes the legal standards discussed in Sections II through VI and maps them onto the specific claims and factual allegations in the Complaint. The discussion is organized by Count.

**[A. Count I --- Monopolization (Sherman Act § 2)]**

Count I is vulnerable on multiple grounds. First, the Complaint\'s market definition is facially deficient in both its product and geographic dimensions. The product market --- "commercially insured orthopedic surgery and related services" --- excludes 44% of orthopedic procedures performed in the Tri-County Area that are paid for by government payers (Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA). The Complaint offers no justification for this exclusion, despite the obvious interchangeability of the services regardless of payer type. The geographic market --- limited to Sullivan, Washington, and Carter Counties, Tennessee --- ignores the readily accessible Bristol, Virginia/Abingdon, Virginia corridor (approximately 25 miles north) and the Asheville, North Carolina regional medical hub (approximately 65 miles southeast). The absence of any allegations regarding cross-border competition or patient travel patterns renders the geographic market definition unsupported and likely gerrymandered.

Second, the Complaint\'s market share allegations are internally inconsistent and, even at their highest, insufficient to support an inference of monopoly power. Paragraph 47 alleges "approximately 70%" of procedures, while Paragraph 83 alleges "over 60%" of revenue. Under *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, the court need not credit contradictory allegations. Moreover, even the higher figure --- approximately 70% --- falls below the threshold at which courts have found monopoly power; the weight of authority holds that shares below 75% are per se insufficient absent compelling additional evidence of barriers to entry. The Complaint alleges no meaningful barriers to entry --- and the existence of four independent surgeons who obtained Tier 1 status through individual negotiations affirmatively suggests that barriers to preferred-network entry are low.

Third, the alleged exclusionary conduct --- offering a 22% discount to insurers in exchange for preferred provider status and tiered copay structures --- is procompetitive on its face. The PPCAs reduce costs for consumers, which is the type of conduct the antitrust laws are designed to protect. The tiered structure does not foreclose competitors from the market: seven of twelve Plaintiffs remain in-network, and four independent surgeons have obtained Tier 1 status. This is preferential tiering, not exclusionary conduct.

**[B. Count II --- Attempted Monopolization (Sherman Act § 2)]**

Count II is independently vulnerable on the specific intent element. The Complaint contains no direct evidence of anticompetitive intent --- no internal communications, strategic documents, or executive statements evidencing a purpose to exclude competitors. The allegations of intent are entirely inferential, derived from the structure and timing of the PPCAs. But entering into discount agreements with willing insurer counterparties is procompetitive conduct from which anticompetitive intent cannot plausibly be inferred. Under *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, conclusory allegations of intent --- which is all the Complaint offers --- must be disregarded. The remaining factual allegations describe ordinary competitive conduct that does not support a plausible inference of specific intent to monopolize.

The dangerous probability element fails for the same reasons that monopoly power fails under Count I. Without a properly defined relevant market and plausible market share allegations, there is no basis for assessing whether Crestline had a realistic probability of achieving monopoly power. The market definition deficiencies identified in connection with Count I apply with equal force here.

**[C. Count III --- Unreasonable Restraint of Trade (Sherman Act § 1)]**

Count III faces several independent obstacles. First, the PPCAs are vertical agreements --- between a provider (Crestline) and payers (the three insurers) --- not horizontal agreements among competitors. No horizontal conspiracy is alleged. Under *Leegin*, vertical restraints are evaluated under the rule of reason, which requires Plaintiffs to allege net anticompetitive effects in a properly defined market. The Complaint does not satisfy this burden.

Second, the PPCAs do not constitute exclusive dealing. They do not prohibit the insurers from contracting with non-Crestline orthopedic providers. They create a tiered copay structure --- \$25 for Tier 1, \$75 for Tier 2 --- that provides Crestline with a competitive advantage but does not foreclose rivals from the market. Seven of twelve Plaintiff surgeons remain in-network. Four independent surgeons hold Tier 1 status. This is preferential tiering, not exclusive dealing.

Third, even if the PPCAs were characterized as exclusive dealing, their short duration and easy terminability substantially mitigate any foreclosure concern. The PPCAs have three-year initial terms with automatic one-year renewals, terminable by either party on 180 days\' notice. Under *Tampa Electric*, *CDC Technologies*, *Omega Environmental*, and *Concord Boat*, short-term, terminable arrangements are presumptively lawful or at minimum present substantially reduced competitive concern.

Fourth, the Complaint fails to allege any consumer harm. The exclusive form of injury alleged is a \$10.3 million decline in the Plaintiffs\' revenue. There is no allegation that patient prices have increased --- the PPCAs appear to have reduced copays for Tier 1 services. There is no allegation that quality of care has declined. There is no allegation that the total volume of orthopedic services in the Tri-County Area has decreased. The antitrust laws protect competition, not competitors, and an exclusive allegation of competitor harm is insufficient to state a Section 1 claim under the rule of reason.

Fifth, the existence of four independent orthopedic surgeons who have obtained Tier 1 preferred status through individual negotiations with the insurers directly undercuts the foreclosure narrative. If independent surgeons can and do obtain Tier 1 status, the PPCAs are not foreclosing competitors from access to commercially insured patients --- they are merely establishing competitive conditions under which providers must negotiate for preferred terms.

**[D. Antitrust Standing --- All Counts]**

As an alternative basis for dismissal, we should argue that the twelve individual surgeon-Plaintiffs lack antitrust standing under the *AGC* efficient enforcer framework. The Plaintiffs are not parties to the PPCAs. Their injury is indirect --- it flows through the insurers\' independent network design decisions and patients\' independent choices in response to copay differentials. AMP, the institutional competitor with direct contractual relationships to the three insurers, is a more direct victim of the alleged conduct but has elected not to sue. Permitting the individual surgeons to proceed as plaintiffs creates risks of duplicative recovery (if AMP later sues) and complex damages apportionment (among twelve surgeons with varying specialties, volumes, and payer mixes). These factors weigh against antitrust standing and provide an independent ground for dismissal across all three Counts.

**[VIII. Conclusion and Recommendations]**

The Complaint filed by Dr. Vogler and the eleven co-Plaintiffs is vulnerable to dismissal on multiple independent grounds. Based on the research and analysis set forth in this memorandum, I recommend that we structure Crestline\'s Rule 12(b)(6) motion around the following arguments, ranked by anticipated strength:

**Strongest Arguments:**

1\. **Deficient market definition (both product and geographic).** The exclusion of 44% of orthopedic procedures (government-payer volume) from the product market and the exclusion of accessible adjacent geographic areas (Bristol/Abingdon, VA; Asheville, NC) from the geographic market are analytically unjustified and render the market definition facially implausible. Without a properly defined market, all three Counts fail.

2\. **The PPCAs are preferential tiering, not exclusive dealing.** The PPCAs do not prohibit insurers from contracting with non-Crestline providers. Seven Plaintiffs remain in-network. Four independent surgeons hold Tier 1 status. The Complaint describes a competitive advantage, not market foreclosure.

3\. **No consumer harm / no antitrust injury.** The Complaint alleges only a revenue decline suffered by the Plaintiff surgeons. There is no allegation of harm to consumers --- no price increases, no quality reductions, no output limitations. Under *Brunswick* and *NicSand*, this is harm to competitors, not to competition.

4\. **Short-term, terminable agreements defeat foreclosure.** Three-year terms with 180-day termination provisions are the type of short-duration, easily terminable arrangements that courts have held are presumptively lawful or present substantially reduced anticompetitive concern.

5\. **No specific intent for attempted monopolization.** The Complaint concedes the absence of direct evidence and relies entirely on inferences from procompetitive conduct.

**Additional Strong Arguments:**

6\. **Inconsistent market share allegations** undermine plausibility of monopoly power (70% vs. 60%).

7\. **Vertical restraint framework** requires rule of reason analysis, which Plaintiffs cannot satisfy without allegations of net anticompetitive effects.

8\. **Procompetitive justifications** are apparent from the face of the Complaint: the PPCAs produce lower patient copays and reduced costs.

9\. **Questionable antitrust standing** for individual surgeons under the *AGC* factors, particularly given AMP\'s absence as a plaintiff.

10\. **Independent surgeons with Tier 1 status** directly undercut the foreclosure narrative.

**Recommended Structure of the Motion.** I recommend leading with the market definition argument and the tiering-versus-exclusion distinction, as these are the two most compelling and doctrinally clean grounds for dismissal. The antitrust injury/consumer harm argument should follow as a third major pillar. Each Count should then be addressed systematically, with the standing argument presented as an alternative ground applicable to all Counts.

**Caveat on Market Share Threshold.** The research summarized in Section III.A above suggests that courts generally require approximately 70% or higher market share to infer monopoly power, with some decisions requiring higher shares and others --- depending on the strength of evidence regarding barriers to entry and other competitive conditions --- finding monopoly power at somewhat lower levels. I recommend that the motion argue the Complaint\'s internally inconsistent allegations (70% vs. 60%) fail to plausibly allege monopoly power, but that we avoid asserting a rigid numerical threshold in the brief, since the law is somewhat fact-dependent and an overly rigid position could invite unnecessary pushback from the court.

**Briefing Schedule.** The motion to dismiss is due July 8, 2024. Plaintiffs\' opposition is due August 12, 2024. Our reply brief is due September 3, 2024. I will have a draft motion and memorandum in support for your review by June 28, 2024.

**Recommendation.** I recommend requesting dismissal with prejudice on all three Counts. Given the multiple structural deficiencies in the Complaint --- particularly the market definition failures and the absence of any consumer harm allegation --- amendment would likely be futile, and dismissal with prejudice is warranted.

*This memorandum is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. Do not distribute outside the firm without authorization.*
